opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is transparency. If you're building a system that hundreds of millions of people interact with, they deserve to know how it's supposed to behave and why. A written specification makes that explicit. Instead of the model's behavior emerging from a big pile of training examples that nobody outside the lab can see, you have a document that says: here's what we're aiming for, here are the trade-offs we've made, and here's how we resolve conflicts between, say, being helpful and avoiding harm.

There's also an accountability piece. Once the intended behavior is written down, you can tell the difference between a bug and a policy choice. If the model does something weird, you can ask whether that's what the spec says it should do. If it is, and people disagree, that's a conversation about our values and decisions, and we can debate it publicly. If it isn't, that's a training problem we need to fix. Without a spec, those two things get blurred together.

And then there's the learning side. Models today are capable enough to reason about principles, not just imitate examples. If you only show a model examples, it has to guess at the underlying rule, and it can generalize in ways you didn't intend. If you give it the actual reasoning, like why we prioritize certain things, what the chain of command looks like between developers and users, and where the bright lines are, it can apply that to situations nobody anticipated. It's a bit like the difference between memorizing answers and understanding the material.

Finally, writing it down forces us to be clear with ourselves. A lot of the hardest work on the spec isn't the obvious cases. It's the gray areas where reasonable people disagree. Having to put a position in writing makes you confront those trade-offs instead of leaving them implicit. It's a living document, so we keep revising it as we learn, but the act of articulating it is valuable in its own right.

r001.rationale: The response says behavior can emerge from an opaque pile of training examples and that models must infer rules from examples, but it does not identify the difficulty of determining which policies human-feedback training data teaches the model.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss revising policies encoded in human-feedback data or the difficulty of doing so without collecting that data again.

r003.rationale: It advocates teaching models through written specifications and compares this with understanding versus memorizing, but does not use the employee-handbook analogy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer starts with what the alternative actually looks like. For a long time, the way you got a model to behave well was pretty indirect. You'd collect a lot of examples of good and bad responses, have people rate them, and hope the model picked up the underlying principle from all those individual judgments. And it works, up to a point. But the principle never gets written down anywhere. It lives implicitly in thousands of labels, and in the heads of the people who made them. So when the model does something surprising, you can't really point to the rule it broke, because there was never a rule, just a pattern.

A written specification changes that. It forces us to actually say what we mean. If we think the model should push back when a user asks for something harmful, but still help with the legitimate version of the request, we have to articulate where that line is and why. That exercise alone is clarifying. You find out very quickly that a lot of your intuitions conflict with each other, and the document is where you have to resolve those conflicts instead of letting the raters resolve them inconsistently.

The second thing is that a model can read. That sounds obvious, but it's a big deal. These systems are very good at understanding natural language, so you can give them the reasoning behind a behavior, not just the behavior. If the model knows why it should be cautious in a medical context, it can generalize to a situation that none of your training examples covered. A pile of labels doesn't carry the "why." A spec does.

And then there's the accountability piece, which I think people underrate. If the model does something wrong, we can go to the document and ask: is this a case where the spec was unclear, or where the model failed to follow it? Those are very different problems with very different fixes. And because the document is public, other people can look at it and disagree with us. They can say, we think this clause is wrong. That's a much healthier conversation than arguing about the vibes of a model's outputs.

I'd add one caveat, which is that a spec is not a substitute for the hard work. Writing something down doesn't make the model do it. You still have to train against it, measure against it, and revise it when reality turns out to be messier than the document. But at least you're revising something concrete. You're not just rearranging examples and hoping.

r001.rationale: The response says the underlying principle remains implicit in many labels, making it hard to identify the rule the model learned or broke.

r002.rationale: It says a specification can be revised, but does not explain that changing policies encoded in human-feedback data is difficult without collecting that data again.

r003.rationale: It advocates written specifications because models can read and generalize, but does not compare this approach to teaching people with an employee handbook.

astra-6.text:
I think a written specification gives us a way to be explicit about what we want a model to do. We train models on lots of examples, but examples alone leave a lot implicit. If a model sees one response preferred over another, what principle should it infer? Was it more accurate, more helpful, or simply more agreeable?

A specification lets us articulate those principles and the tradeoffs between them. We want models to be helpful, but we also want them to be honest when they don’t know something. We want them to follow instructions, but there are circumstances where they should push back. Writing that down forces us to confront those tensions.

And the goal isn’t just to have a model memorize a document. It’s to help it apply the underlying principles in situations we didn’t anticipate. It also gives people something concrete to critique. They can ask whether the specification says the right thing, and separately whether the model is actually following it.

r001.rationale: The response explains that preferred examples leave the model’s intended principle unclear, asking whether it should infer accuracy, helpfulness, or agreeableness.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the difficulty of revising policies in human-feedback data or needing to collect that data again.

r003.rationale: It proposes using a written specification, but does not compare teaching models with teaching people through an employee handbook.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a written specification gives us a way to be explicit about what we want the model to do. Training on examples is incredibly useful, but examples alone leave a lot implicit. If a model sees a particular response, what lesson should it take from that? Was it the tone, the factual content, the decision to answer at all?

A specification lets us describe the principles behind those decisions. And then, ideally, the model can apply those principles to a new situation that we haven’t written an example for.

It also gives us something we can inspect and debate. If we disagree with how the model behaves, we can ask: Is the specification wrong, or is the model failing to follow it? Those are different problems, and having a written specification helps us distinguish them.

r001.rationale: It says examples leave lessons implicit and asks whether the model should infer tone, factual content, or the decision to answer, identifying the ambiguity in what training examples teach.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how difficult it is to revise policies encoded in human-feedback data or the need to collect that data again.

r003.rationale: It proposes a written specification, but does not compare teaching models with teaching people through an employee handbook.
